profile.name: Matachines
profile.tagline: A ritual sword-dance of European origin adapted by Native and Mestizo communities.
profile.insight: In Bernalillo, New Mexico, Matachines dancers have performed for over three hundred years to enact the ancient battle between good and evil.
profile.profile: The Matachines are a tradition of ritual dancers found from Peru up to northern New Mexico, blending European sword-dance roots with Indigenous practices. Emerging in Spain during the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries from traditions like the moresca, the dance was introduced to the Americas by Spanish missionaries as an evangelizing tool. Performers wear ceremonial attire and masks to enact narratives featuring characters such as El Monarca, La Malinche, and El Toro. Today, the societies dance to venerate saints, Mother Mary, or the Holy Trinity while celebrating native peoples' faith and culture.
profile.profile_long:
The Matachines dance emerged in Europe during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, closely related to the moresca and the bouffons described by Thoinot Arbeau in his 1589 Orchésographie. In 1642, Juan de Esquivel Navarro documented the tradition in his treatise Discursos sobre el arte del dançado. A sword dance resembling a matachin was even performed at Hampton Court on January 6, 1604, by Scottish courtiers before James VI and I and the French ambassador. Transported to the Americas by Spanish missionaries, the dance served as an evangelizing tool, introduced as the Dance of the Moors and Christians. In Bernalillo, New Mexico, the Matachines de San Lorenzo have maintained continuous performances for more than three hundred years.

The dance features a distinct cast of characters dressed in ceremonial attire. El Monarca typically represents Moctezuma or another tribal leader, supported by two to four captains acting as main generals. La Malinche appears as the Native or Mestizo woman, while El Toro symbolizes the malevolent comic man or Satan, draped in buffalo skins and wearing the horns of a sacred ancestor. Alongside Abuelo and Abuela—the grandfather and grandmother—and a chorus of dancers, the performance portrays Moctezuma's desertion of his people, his luring back by La Malinche's smiles, the eventual reunion, and the final slaying of El Toro, who is blamed for all mischief.

While oral history among Pueblo tribes connects the dance to the Moors and Christians, its significance transformed outside the Iberian peninsula. Participants dance for profound religious purposes, venerating Mother Mary—such as Our Lady of Guadalupe—local saints, Christ, or the Holy Trinity, represented by a three-forked Sword of the Holy Trinity. All cultural artifacts associated with the performance are explicitly blessed by a priest. The fundamental narrative opposes good and evil, with good ultimately prevailing, serving as a celebration of native peoples and their salvation through faith and culture.

Performers wear traditional ceremonial clothing, with masks that vary significantly from village to village and tribe to tribe. In central Mexico, the tradition is also known as matlachines and matlatzines. From the Yaqui communities to the Pueblos of New Mexico and southward into Peru, the dance has adapted to local cultures while maintaining recognizable formations. Though dance steps differ among distinct peoples, the spatial formations remain broadly similar, reflecting a shared historical root forged in colonial encounters.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance emerged in Spain in the early 17th century, inspired by European traditions like the moresca, and was documented in 1642 by Juan de Esquivel Navarro. It was imported into Latin America and the Southwestern United States by Spanish missionaries as an evangelizing tool known as the Dance of the Moors and Christians. In Bernalillo, New Mexico, the Matachines de San Lorenzo have performed for over three hundred years.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves a chorus of dancers alongside specific characters performing formations that are all similar, though individual dance steps vary among different peoples and villages.
sections.music_and_instruments: The tradition is accompanied by characteristic music associated with the danza de matachines, though specific instruments are not detailed in the sources beyond historical mentions of flutes in ancient variants.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional ceremonial dress and masks that vary in style from village to village. El Toro wears buffalo skins and the horns of a sacred ancestor. All cultural artifacts associated with the dance are blessed by a priest.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance serves a deeper religious purpose to venerate Mother Mary, local saints, Christ, or the Holy Trinity. It functions as a celebration of native peoples in the Americas and their salvation through unity of faith and culture, portraying the triumph of good over evil.
sections.notable_figures: Chief characters include El Monarca (Moctezuma or another tribal leader), the captains, La Malinche (the Native or Mestizo woman), El Toro (representing Satan), and the grandparents Abuelo and Abuela.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is found from Peru up to northern New Mexico, and is written as matlachines and matlatzines in central Mexico. Styles vary by village and tribe, including notable practices among Pueblo tribes and Yaqui communities.
sections.lineage: Derived from European traditions such as the moresca and the bouffons documented in 16th and 17th-century Europe, adapted by Indigenous and Mestizo societies in the Americas.

profile.sacred_note: The dance serves a deep religious purpose to venerate saints, Mother Mary, and the Holy Trinity, and all associated cultural artifacts are blessed by a priest.
